big_idea: AREA is the SPACE INSIDE a shape. Compare by MATCHING, COVERING, or DECOMPOSING.
learning_intention: We are learning to compare areas of shapes by matching or covering.
student_learning_goal: I can compare areas of shapes by matching or covering.
success_criteria: I can SAY what area means.
I can COVER a shape with tiles.
I can COMPARE 2 shapes by area.
I can EXPLAIN gaps and overlaps.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Roo the Ruler Rabbit — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Roo: AREA is HOW MUCH space is INSIDE. Cover the field with tiles to compare! Roo opens: 'ROWS times COLUMNS — that's AREA!' Yesterday Roo did the BOUNDARY. Today we cover the INSIDE.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Roo the Ruler Rabbit puppet. 'Measurement friends — yesterday we measured AROUND. Today we measure INSIDE — that's AREA!'

Define. 'AREA = space INSIDE a shape. We COVER with tiles to measure.'

Demo. 'Two fields. Field A: 6 tiles. Field B: 8 tiles. B has MORE area!'

3 ways to compare:
1. MATCH (place one shape on top of other — bigger sticks out).
2. COVER (count tiles inside each).
3. DECOMPOSE (cut and rearrange — same total area).

Demo each:
- MATCH: Two same-size squares match perfectly = same area.
- COVER: Rectangle 3×2 = 6 tiles. Square 2×2 = 4 tiles. Rectangle bigger.
- DECOMPOSE: Cut a rectangle into 2 triangles, rearrange. Same area!

'Roo says — different shapes can have the SAME area!'

Now gaps and overlaps. 'When we cover, tiles must NOT overlap (count too many) and NOT have gaps (count too few). Tile EDGE-TO-EDGE.'

Demo bad covering. 'Look — 4 tiles with overlaps says 4 but really 3.5. Or 4 tiles with gaps says 4 but really 5.'

'Roo says — accurate covering means tiles TOUCH but don't OVERLAP.'

Now each pair gets 4 shape outlines + 30 square tiles. They cover and count.

'Roo says — count carefully!'

steps.instruction: Hand out shape outlines + 30 tiles. Pairs cover each shape.
Compare 2 pairs of shapes — which has bigger area?
Stretch: decompose 1 shape into smaller parts and recompose.

STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share their area methods — Pair A counts one-by-one; Pair B uses rows × columns. Class compares which is faster + more reliable for a 6×4 rectangle. Cite Battista (1999) spatial structuring.
steps.teacher_prompt: Roo: 'Counting works for small. ROWS × COLUMNS works for ANY size.'

differentiation.for_extending: Find 2 different shapes with same area.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Five signals: covers; counts; compares; explains gaps; consistency.

discussion_prompts: How is area DIFFERENT from perimeter?
Can 2 shapes have the same area?
consolidation.exit_routine: Roo's area chant — 'Roo says: ROWS times COLUMNS — that's AREA!' (3x). Each child computes one area using array structure.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child loses the array structure — repairing the spatial structuring trap
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On comparing areas, the dominant Grade-3 trap is the SPATIAL STRUCTURING failure (Battista 1999, 'Spatial Structuring in Geometric Reasoning'; Outhred & Mitchelmore 2000 on rectangle area): child counts cells one-by-one without seeing the array (rows × columns) structure. Without it, area comparison cannot be done efficiently.

Yesterday Roo did perimeter (boundary). Today we compare AREAS (interior coverage). Lesson 3 introduces square cm; Lesson 4 capacity/mass; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Cover activity. Child has tiles overlapping by 1 tile width.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Roo asks — are your tiles TOUCHING? Any GAPS?'

Probe. 'Find an overlap. Fix it. Find a gap. Fill it.'

Generalise. 'Roo says — accurate AREA means tiles fit edge-to-edge. No gaps, no overlaps.'

If still careless: trace tile boundaries with finger. 'Each tile in its own SPOT.'
common_misconceptions: Tile gaps = small effect. (Repair: every gap = under-count.)
Overlap = double count. (Repair: yes — also wrong.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child counts cells one-by-one: drill 'find ROWS and COLUMNS first; multiply'; child re-counts using array structure.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child uses array but loses count: chunk in 5s or 10s; row × column visualization.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child applies array correctly but cannot articulate: force 'area = ROWS × COLUMNS = ___ × ___ = ___ square units.'

parts_outline.task: Compare 2 shape pairs: bigger or smaller area.
Find 2 different shapes with the SAME area.
